query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nano-engineered graded copper interlayer at the tungsten–copper interface will create a seamless heterointerface that enhances thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance in W–Cu composites.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional W–Cu metal-matrix composite with distinct tungsten and copper phases separated by an interface that exhibits relatively high thermal resistance.
generation.intervention: Deposit a graded copper interlayer at the tungsten–copper boundaries to form a continuous, well-bonded interface.
generation.conditions: Under high heat-dissipation loads and typical fusion reactor joint operating conditions, including cyclic temperature fluctuations and irradiation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The seamless heterointerface provided by the graded copper interlayer, which minimizes discontinuities between tungsten and copper.
generation.mechanism: The graded copper layer reduces interfacial thermal resistance by achieving a continuous lattice transition between tungsten and copper, thereby enhancing phonon-mediated heat transfer. Simultaneously, the robust interface is expected to maintain mechanical integrity and resist irradiation-induced defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: W–Cu composites with the graded copper interlayer will display higher thermal conductivity compared to standard composites, and they will maintain comparable or improved mechanical durability and irradiation resistance under extreme operational conditions.
generation.baseline: Standard W–Cu composites without the graded copper interlayer, which typically suffer from higher interfacial thermal resistance and may exhibit degradation in durability and irradiation resistance under severe conditions.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected as long as the copper interlayer remains continuous and well-adhered under operational stresses. Excessively high irradiation doses or thermal cycles that compromise the integrity of the interlayer may negate the performance gains.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain whether the interface engineering strategy, proven in Cu-modified graphitic films for enhanced thermal management, will fully translate to the metal–matrix system in terms of irradiation resistance, as direct evidence in W–Cu composites is lacking.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set with the graded copper interlayer and one control set without it. Subject both sets to cyclic thermal shock between 77 K and 300 K and to irradiation doses typical of fusion reactor conditions.
measurements: Thermal conductivity before and after cyclic testing
Mechanical durability tests (e.g., tensile strength, impact resistance)
Microstructural analysis of the tungsten–copper interface using TEM or SEM
Irradiation resistance assessed via defect density measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the composites with the graded copper interlayer do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in thermal conductivity while maintaining mechanical and irradiation performance comparable to or better than the control samples, the hypothesis is considered falsified.

Highlights Presenting the first investigation into the structurally bubbling-failure mechanism of graphitic film during cyclic liquid nitrogen shocks.Proposing an innovative design about seamless heterointerface constructing a Cu-modified structure.Inventing a new ultra-stable species of highly thermally conductive films to inspire new techniques for efficient and extreme thermal management.Supplementary InformationThe online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s40820-023-01277-1.Keywords: Highly thermally conductive, Structurally ultra-stable, Graphitic film, Extreme thermal management, Liquid nitrogen bubbling AbstractHighly thermally conductive graphitic film (GF) materials have become a competitive solution for the thermal management of high-power electronic devices. However, their catastrophic structural failure under extreme alternating thermal/cold shock poses a significant challenge to reliability and safety. Here, we present the first investigation into the structural failure mechanism of GF during cyclic liquid nitrogen shocks (LNS), which reveals a bubbling process characterized by “permeation-diffusion-deformation” phenomenon.
